title: Design an agent system that turns specs into prototypes
description: A system that turns an approved spec into a working prototype your team can react to right away.

prd.title: PRD (Product Requirements Document)
prd.content: A structured spec for something you want built: the problem, the users, what it must do, what's out of scope. Producing a PRD first and handing it to Claude Code beats describing the build conversationally — the requirements survive the whole session.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

react.title: React
react.content: A JavaScript library for building interactive user interfaces out of reusable pieces called components. Most modern web apps you use daily — Notion, Linear, ChatGPT — are built in React.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

stack.title: Stack
stack.content: The set of tools something is built with or that you work with. An app's stack is its languages and services, from database to frontend (the Leland Courses stack is Astro, Tailwind, Cloudflare, and Supabase). Your AI stack is the toolkit you've assembled for your own work — chat tools, agents, automations, and the connectors that tie them together.

branch.title: Branch
branch.content: A parallel version of your repo where you can make changes without touching the main version — like working on a draft copy. When Claude experiments with a fix, it usually creates a branch first so the main version stays clean until you approve.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

deploy.title: Deploy / Deployment
deploy.content: Taking code that works on your computer and making it live on a server so others can access it via the internet. When Claude 'deploys' a site, it's publishing it to the web.

github.title: GitHub
github.content: A website where you store and share Git repositories online. Used in this program as your AI working directory — a central place for your files that Claude can access from anywhere.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

vercel.title: Vercel
vercel.content: A hosting platform optimized for modern web apps, especially Next.js. Pushes to GitHub deploy automatically with preview URLs for every change. Popular choice for students shipping AI-powered web apps in Level 3 and beyond.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

handoff.title: Handoff
handoff.content: When your main agent passes a job to a sub-agent and waits for the result. Cleaner than mixing two agents' contexts in one thread, and the moment to inspect for prompt injection if either agent is reading untrusted input.

sandbox.title: Sandbox
sandbox.content: An isolated environment where software runs without affecting the rest of your computer. Claude's Cowork mode runs in a sandboxed virtual machine — a safety feature that keeps automated work contained.

markdown.title: Markdown
markdown.content: A lightweight text formatting language using simple symbols: # for headings, \*\* for bold, - for bullet points. Your CLAUDE.md, skill files, and voice guides are written in Markdown.

terminal.title: Terminal
terminal.content: A text-based interface for controlling your computer by typing commands instead of clicking. Also called the command line or CLI. On Mac: open with Cmd + Space and type 'Terminal.' Claude Code runs inside the terminal.

workflow.title: Workflow
workflow.content: A multi-step process Claude runs to accomplish a goal — for example: read emails → filter by topic → summarize → post to Slack. Workflows can be run manually or on a schedule.

anthropic.title: Anthropic
anthropic.content: The company that created Claude. An AI safety company focused on building reliable, interpretable AI systems.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: A spec sitting in a doc waits for an engineering cycle that might be weeks out. This system skips the wait. Once a spec clears review, a coding [agent](#tooltip-agent) reads it and builds a working prototype the team can [react](#tooltip-react) to before that meeting ends.

At Chime, a PM writes a [PRD](#tooltip-prd) in [markdown](#tooltip-markdown), opens a [terminal](#tooltip-terminal), and runs a coding agent against it. Twenty minutes later the PRD is running software, per [Builder.io's writeup by Vishwas Gopinath](https://www.builder.io/blog/claude-code-for-product-managers). [Anthropic](#tooltip-anthropic) treats this as a distinct PM skill too, naming "turning an approved spec into a prototype" a starter [workflow](#tooltip-workflow) built for people who don't write code day to day, in its [Product Management Plugin](https://claude.com/plugins/product-management).

This works as a one-time paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) each time a spec clears review, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill) your whole team reuses, or an agent triggered automatically whenever a spec is marked approved in your ticketing tool. Every version builds in a [sandbox](#tooltip-sandbox), isolated from production.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming how detailed your specs are, what kind of prototype you need, the [stack](#tooltip-stack) it's built in, and how you plan to review it.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that turns an approved spec into a working prototype. Ask me questions, one at a time, about how detailed my specs are, what kind of prototype I need, what stack it's built in, and how I plan to review it. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces decisions you didn't know you needed to make, and the scope document becomes the brief for every prototype after it.

items: Whether this builds inside an existing codebase or starts from scratch.
What counts as done, a throwaway demo or something engineering can build on later.
Which design system the prototype needs to match, if any.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are code hosting for the [branch](#tooltip-branch) itself ([GitHub](#tooltip-github)), a design tool for visual fidelity (Figma), and a [deployment](#tooltip-deploy) sandbox for review ([Vercel](#tooltip-vercel)). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on the approved spec. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Turn an approved spec into a working prototype for review.

Context: [Paste your approved spec or PRD. Note your target platform or stack, e.g. "React web app" or "iOS Swift," and any existing design system it needs to match.]

Rules:
- Build only what the spec explicitly describes.
- Flag anything ambiguous instead of guessing at it.
- Keep the prototype in a separate branch or sandbox. Never touch production.
- Note what was built, what was skipped, and what still needs an engineer's judgment.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming the branch and sandbox constraint up front keeps the agent from wandering into production, and the built/skipped/needs-judgment split keeps the [handoff](#tooltip-handoff) to engineering honest.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Did it build only what the spec described, flag ambiguity instead of guessing, and leave production untouched?
**Feedback.** Correct the rules by hand so the next spec doesn't hit the same guess.

items: Chain this off an idea-to-PRD build so specs flow straight into prototypes.
Check the finished build against the original acceptance criteria before handoff.
Log what got prototyped against what shipped.

children.text: **Measure** with a concrete [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft the rubric and run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each prototype, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for spec name, date built, what was built, what was flagged as ambiguous, and what engineering changed before shipping. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks catch scope creep before a reviewer has to hunt for it, and the run log shows which kinds of specs come back clean.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few runs straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that keeps failing is a skill candidate. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. A coding agent will build past the spec's scope if left unchecked, so the run needs a stop-and-ask rule for ambiguity, and engineering still reviews the result before anything gets near production.
